title: Building a Truth Table
short: A formula with n letters has 2ⁿ rows; list them in a fixed order and fill a column for each part, ending with the main connective.
trouble: Learners miss rows or repeat them. Halve the pattern for each letter: T T F F, then T F T F.

blocks.html: In Computing a Truth Value you found a formula's value in one row. A truth table does that for every possible row at once, so you can see everything a formula can do.

A formula with $n$ different letters needs $2^n$ rows. List them in the standard order: the first letter is T for the first half of the rows and F for the second half; each later letter halves the block size; the last letter alternates T, F. Then fill a column for each part, ending with the main connective.

Each letter can be T or F independently. With one letter that gives 2 cases; adding a letter doubles the count, because each old case splits into one with the new letter T and one with it F. So 2 letters give 4 rows, 3 give 8, and 4 give 16. The standard order is simply a way to write all of them with no repeats and no gaps.

blocks.title: How many rows?
blocks.q: How many rows does the table for $(p \land q) \to (r \lor \neg p)$ need?
steps: Count the different letters: $p$, $q$, $r$. Repeats of $p$ do not count again.

blocks.title: Build a small table
steps: Column $\neg q$: F, T, F, T.
Column $p \to \neg q$: T→F is F; T→T is T; F→F is T; F→T is T.

blocks.title: Read a value
blocks.q: In the standard order for $p$, $q$, $r$, what is $q$ in row 6?
steps: $q$ runs in blocks of 2: T T F F T T F F.
Rows 5 and 6 make up the third block of two, and that block is T T.

blocks.html: Missing rows or repeating them, which happens when the rows are written in no fixed order. Use the halving pattern every time: for three letters, write $p$ as TTTTFFFF, $q$ as TTFFTTFF and $r$ as TFTFTFTF. Then count: the table must have exactly $2^n$ rows.

items: Count the letters and write $2^n$ rows in the standard order.
Add a column for each part, from the smallest outward.
Fill each column from the columns it depends on.
The last column, under the main connective, is the answer.

blocks.html: Truth tables can grow large, but they never fail: a table always answers the question it is asked. That is why the next topics use them to decide whether a formula is always true, whether two formulas agree, and whether an argument is valid.
